section_summary: The section closes a translated appeal in an Ohama coal mine labor case, gives the Japanese Supreme Court’s decision dismissing that appeal, and includes Japanese-language copies of the decision and appeal arguments. The remaining documents trace a 1949 State Department dispute over an Australian proposal to extend labor rights to workers in Japanese government enterprises, including exchanges with SCAP and reports of Soviet press coverage.

subfiles.title: Translated grounds of appeal in the Ohama coal mine case, conclusion
subfiles.about: Counsel argues that suspensions and dismissals responded to miners’ sabotage rather than an intent to suppress the union.
subfiles.summary: The concluding page asks that the earlier decision be reversed for misreading the law and failing to determine who was responsible for sabotage.

subfiles.title: Supreme Court decision in Shigemori’s labor-law appeal, English translation
subfiles.from: Second Petty Bench, Supreme Court of Japan
subfiles.about: The court dismisses Shigemori’s appeal over suspensions and dismissals of Ohama mine union members.
subfiles.summary: The court holds that the employer punished protected union activity and weakened the unions, even if some workers also engaged in illegal sabotage. It rejects arguments based on a closed-shop agreement, the union’s demands, and the claimed absence of economic injury.

subfiles.title: Japanese text of the Supreme Court decision
subfiles.from: Second Petty Bench, Supreme Court of Japan
subfiles.about: The Japanese-language decision rejects the appeal concerning treatment of Ohama coal mine union members.
subfiles.summary: The original-language decision addresses the mine’s suspensions and dismissals, the employees’ union expulsions, and whether the employer’s actions unlawfully penalized a labor dispute. It concludes by dismissing the appeal.

subfiles.title: Japanese grounds of appeal in the Ohama coal mine case
subfiles.about: Defense counsel challenges the finding that Shigemori unlawfully suspended and dismissed union members.
subfiles.summary: The lengthy Japanese appeal argues that mine workers’ slowdown and sabotage justified disciplinary action and disputes the lower court’s finding of an intent to weaken the unions. It also challenges the treatment of office employees, the assessment of the union’s demands, and the evidence supporting the judgment.

subfiles.title: Urgent routing note to Hickerson
subfiles.about: Smith asks whether an attached memorandum can be added to a memorandum for the Secretary’s staff.
subfiles.summary: An urgent request to forward an attached memorandum.

subfiles.title: Urgent routing note to Hickerson, revised wording
subfiles.about: Smith asks whether, absent objection, an attached memorandum may be sent to the Secretary’s staff that afternoon.
subfiles.summary: A revised request to forward the attached memorandum.

subfiles.title: File note on Webb’s review
subfiles.about: The note explains why the paper bears no indication that Webb reviewed it.
subfiles.summary: Webb considered the paper with EUR memoranda before the papers were separated and returned.

subfiles.title: Meeting with the Australian Ambassador on June 14
subfiles.about: FE recommends seeking withdrawal or postponement of Australia’s FEC resolution on Japanese government enterprise workers.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum sets out the risks of adopting the Australian resolution or defeating it by a United States veto. It supplies arguments for asking the Australian Ambassador to withdraw or table the measure.

subfiles.title: Australian resolution before the FEC on rights of Japanese government enterprise employees
subfiles.about: Thorp proposes a United States position granting government enterprise workers collective bargaining, mediation, and arbitration, but no right to strike.
subfiles.summary: Thorp argues that the existing treatment of telecommunications workers undermines confidence in SCAP’s labor policy and strengthens Communist appeals to Japanese workers. He recommends seeking agreement at senior levels of the United States government and asking Commonwealth delegates to delay a vote while that position is developed.

subfiles.title: State-Army-Labor message proposing a response to the Australian resolution
subfiles.from: Department of the Army, conveying the State-Army-Labor proposal
subfiles.about: Washington proposes extending collective bargaining rights to all nonexecutive Japanese government enterprise employees while withholding the right to strike.
subfiles.summary: The message asks SCAP to support the principle, including telecommunications workers, so friendly FEC countries might withdraw or table the Australian proposal. It requests urgent comments.

subfiles.title: SCAP reply on labor rights and the Australian FEC proposal
subfiles.about: SCAP rejects the proposed change for telecommunications workers and questions reluctance to veto the Australian resolution.
subfiles.summary: The reply describes telecommunications as essential to Japanese internal security and defends the existing public service laws. It argues that changing the policy would aid Soviet propaganda and urges efforts to have the Australian proposal withdrawn or tabled.

subfiles.title: Exchange of telegrams with SCAP on the labor situation
subfiles.to: FE, Mr. Butterworth and Mr. Allison
subfiles.about: The memorandum reviews and disputes SCAP’s objections to extending collective bargaining rights to telecommunications workers.
subfiles.summary: Point-by-point comments challenge SCAP’s security, legal, and political arguments. The memorandum recommends continued approaches to friendly FEC countries and considers either a veto or a United States counterproposal if Australia persists.

subfiles.title: Note on timing of an approach to SCAP
subfiles.about: The note discusses a proposed approach to SCAP despite current Japanese railway labor disputes.
subfiles.summary: It acknowledges the difficult timing but favors action, noting that the proposed instructions leave SCAP discretion.

subfiles.title: Proposed message from Gray to MacArthur
subfiles.about: A proposed senior-level message asks MacArthur to extend collective bargaining rights to all nonexecutive government enterprise employees.
subfiles.summary: The draft excludes a right to strike and seeks SCAP’s support for persuading friendly FEC members to abandon a labor-rights resolution.

subfiles.title: Labor rights of Japanese government enterprise workers
subfiles.about: Butterworth opposes Thorp’s proposal to raise government workers’ labor rights with SCAP immediately.
subfiles.summary: He argues that a veto of the Australian resolution can be defended and that current strikes make another approach to SCAP ill timed. He recommends withholding the proposed message and senior-level discussions.

subfiles.title: Soviet press report on Japanese labor unrest
subfiles.about: The telegram summarizes Soviet press reports of Japanese reactions to measures against workers and a railway strike.
subfiles.summary: It reports TASS coverage of Japanese public opinion and the railway workers’ strike.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning labor rights of Japanese government enterprise workers
subfiles.about: Thorp accepts delaying a further approach to SCAP while urging later action on defective labor legislation.
subfiles.summary: Thorp leaves the timing to FE and asks Butterworth to reconsider action when feasible.

subfiles.title: Pravda report on Panyushkin’s FEC statement
subfiles.about: The telegram reports Pravda’s coverage of Panyushkin’s criticism of MacArthur’s labor measures.
subfiles.summary: Pravda printed a Washington TASS dispatch on the FEC statement.
